one_liner: A wide-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 2.7x fair value. Interesting below about $290.

profile.what: Costco runs membership warehouse clubs selling groceries, household goods, electronics and fuel in bulk at low prices, with about 900 warehouses worldwide.
profile.money: It marks up goods only slightly over cost, so most of its profit comes from membership fees paid annually by about 80 million paid members, renewing at about 90% in the US and Canada. Low prices drive volume, and volume gives it buying power.
profile.valued: Costco trades at one of the highest P/Es in retail because investors prize its steady growth and loyal members. The multiple leaves little room for disappointment.

summary.sentence: An exceptional retailer with loyal members and one of the most demanding valuations in the market.
strengths: Every financial trend points up, with net cash.
Membership fees make earnings very predictable.
risks: About 50x earnings: the price assumes perfection.
Thin net margin by design fails the mechanical 5% test.
Even small slowdowns could compress the multiple.

meaning.what_it_does: Runs about 900 membership warehouse clubs selling groceries and general merchandise in bulk at very low markups.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Thin profits on merchandise plus high-margin annual membership fees, which make up most of operating income.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Members renew at about 90% because the savings are real; new warehouses add members every year.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Losing its low-price reputation, or management abandoning the frugal culture.

moat.summary: Costco's low prices come from buying volume and low overhead that rivals cannot match without wrecking their own margins.

industry.summary: Groceries and household goods change slowly; Costco's model has worked for decades.

management.summary: A famously owner-oriented culture: rising equity, net cash and special dividends.

financial_health.ratio_gaps: Not available from the data source, so not shown: a ten-year record, inventory and receivables turnover, the quick ratio, goodwill and tangible book value, and maintenance capex split from growth capex. Owner earnings therefore deduct all capex, which is conservative.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow, capex held at depreciation: $9.2B a year: operating cash flow less depreciation and stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). Capex is running at 2.4x depreciation, so most of it is expansion, not upkeep. (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 6–12% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 4%; cost of capital 8.8%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
